outputs.L1: At the stables, each stall was labeled with a name. Biscuit stood aloof — I faced, always and invariably, his clockwork tail. Crab knew the salt lick all too well. Trapezoid had mastered stillness: a midnight mare, she was the sternest and the tallest, her chest straining against the very edges of her stall. I harbored no fear of Never, the chestnut gelding, and so I rode his iron haunches as far as Panther Gap. Never and I lived in Virginia then. We could neither flee nor be kept. Seldom did I reach the little mountain without him, its gentle crests making valleys of the indifferent grasses. What was that low sound I heard, alone with Never? A lone horse, a lodestar, a habit of fear. We think of a horse less as the history of one man and his sorrows than as the history of an entire age of evil. Why I chose Never, I shall never know. I fed him odd lettuce, an abundant bitterness. Who wore the bit and harness, who was the steed made ready. Never took the carrot — words by my own reckoning, an account of creeks and oystercatchers. Our hoof-house rested at the foot of the mountain, upon which rested another house, more brazen than any statuary. Let it be known: I first mistook gelding for gilding. I am the fool who keeps his faith in Never. Somewhere, a golden door, burdened with apology, refuses all mint from the yard.
outputs.L2: In the stable, every stall bore a nameplate. Biscuit kept his distance—what I encountered, time and again without fail, was his mechanical, ever-swishing tail. Crab was overly familiar with the salt lick. Trapezoid had perfected the art of standing motionless: a black mare, the most severe and the highest of them all, with her breast pressing outward toward the boundaries of her enclosure. I felt no fear toward Never, that chestnut gelding, and so I would climb onto his hard hindquarters and ride him all the way to Panther Gap. Back then, Never and I made our home in Virginia. Escape wasn't possible for us, nor was captivity. Rarely could I make it to the small mountain unless he carried me, its gentle ridges turning the ordinary grasses into valleys below. And what was that faint noise that reached my ears when I was by myself with Never? A solitary horse, a guiding star, a familiar pattern of dread. Rather than viewing a horse as the chronicle of a single man's griefs, we see it as the chronicle of an entire wicked era. The reason I settled on Never remains a mystery I'll carry forever. I gave him strange lettuce and plenty of bitterness. Who bore the bit and harness, who served as the willing mount. Never accepted the carrot—phrases counted up in my own way, a ledger of streams and oystercatchers. Our house of hooves sat below the mountain, which held another dwelling bolder than any sculpture. Let this be recorded: at first I confused gelding with gilding. I am the foolish one who trusts in Never. Somewhere a golden door, heavy with regret, turns away every bit of mint offered from the yard.
outputs.L3:
At the stables, every horse arrived already bearing a name, and every name seemed to have summoned a character to match it. There was Biscuit, aloof and indifferent, who regarded the human hand as a curiosity to be tolerated rather than welcomed. There was Trapezoid, the stern and towering midnight mare, so black she seemed cut from the absence of light, whose very geometry of a name suggested something rigid and unyielding. Each animal in its stall held itself apart, a distinct temperament behind the same soft eyes, so that walking the length of the barn was like passing a gallery of private moods.

Among them all, I came to love Never, the chestnut gelding, with a devotion I never planned and could not entirely explain. We went out together through the green folds of Virginia, up toward Panther Gap and the little mountain that rose beyond it, and in those long rides something settled between us, a wordless understanding that asked nothing and gave everything. He carried me as though he had chosen the arrangement himself, and I began to think of him not as an animal I rode but as a companion who happened to bear my weight.

Yet the more time I spent among these horses, the more they came to mean something larger than themselves. I could not look at them as the property of one man or the sorrow of one household. They seemed instead to stand for an entire era, an evil and encompassing historical time whose weight they bore in their patient bodies. A horse, after all, has always been made to labor inside the schemes of men, to be bought and bred and driven, and in their silence I read the long ledger of a whole age rather than any single person's private grief.

Still, I confess I chose Never without reason, or without a reason I could give aloud. I fed him from my own hands, I spoke to him in the low voice one uses for secrets, and I admitted to myself, even as I did it, that I was being a fool. He could not answer me; he could not keep any promise; and yet I kept faith in him as though he were owed it. There is a kind of foolishness that knows itself and continues anyway, and that was mine.

And beneath all of this ran a current of play with words, the way a stream runs beneath a bridge you have crossed a hundred times without looking down. When I first heard the word *gelding*, I heard *gilding*, and the mistake would not leave me. It linked, in my mind, the humble wooden stable with its smell of hay and dust to another structure altogether—a more brazen, gilded house that stood higher up on the mountain, gleaming with a wealth the horses would never share. The slip of a single letter opened a whole comparison: the plain and the gilt, the working animal and the ornamented mansion, the honest and the shining. I kept the error the way I kept faith in Never, knowing it was wrong, unwilling to correct it, because it told me something true.
outputs.L4:
**Never**

There is a horse named Never at the stable in Virginia, and I go to him the way you return to a word you cannot stop mispronouncing. Never, they call across the paddock, and the animal lifts his head as if the negation were only his name and not a whole philosophy. I came here to learn to ride. I stayed to learn the horses' names.

There is Mercy, who bites. There is Sunday, who will not be caught. There is a mare called Ruth, and I think of the field, the gleaning, the woman who said *whither thou goest*, and I press my face to her flank and smell the hay-warm dark of her.

The stable-hand tells me Never is a gelding. For a moment I hear *gilding*, and I see the horse leafed in gold, illuminated like a letter in an old manuscript, the animal made ornament, made holy by a slip of the ear. Then I understand the truer word, the cut word, the word that means something was taken so the beast would be gentle. Gelding. Gilding. What we lose to be led. What we cover in gold to forget the losing.

Fear lives in the body before it lives in the mind. I know this on Never's back, my knees remembering a danger my thoughts have not yet named. The horse feels my fear as weather. He shifts. The old ground of Virginia holds its history the way the horse holds my trembling—patiently, and without forgiveness. Beneath these hooves: tobacco, and the hands that worked it, and the ledgers with names in them, and the fields sown with a grief that still comes up green each spring.

I want to say the bond is simple. A girl, a horse, an afternoon. But nothing here is only itself. Mercy bites. Ruth gleans. Sunday will not be caught, and Never—Never is the answer we give to the question *will it happen again*, the answer we do not believe even as we say it. Never lifts his head. Never comes when called.

Faith, my grandmother said, is the thing you do with your hands when your mind has quit. So I curry the coat. I pick the stones from the hooves. I braid the mane the way you braid time, over and under, holding the loose ends of the days. And the horse, who does not know his name is a vow broken before it was made, leans his great weight against me, and I bear it, and I am borne.

Every small love is freighted. You cannot lay your cheek against a living thing in this particular soil and not feel the whole troubled ground beneath you, tilting, asking to be answered. I have no answer. I have only Never, gilded in the last light, gelded and gentle, letting me sit the fear until it settles into something that could almost be called trust—which is only fear that has agreed, for now, to be ridden.

# The Curious Case of Biscuit the Crab

On a stretch of golden beach where the tide left behind little pools of sparkling water, there lived a small hermit crab named Biscuit. He earned his name because his shell was a warm, sandy brown, round and speckled—exactly like a freshly baked biscuit fresh from the oven.

Biscuit was no ordinary crab. While his brothers and sisters spent their days scuttling sideways and hunting for scraps, Biscuit loved shapes. He would spend hours arranging pebbles and shells into neat patterns along the shoreline.

One sunny morning, Biscuit discovered something wonderful washed up near a tide pool: a piece of driftwood shaped like a **trapezoid**. Its two parallel sides—one long, one short—and its slanted edges fascinated him. He had never seen anything so perfectly geometric in all his days by the sea.

"What a marvelous shape!" Biscuit exclaimed, tapping it with his claw. "One pair of parallel sides. Truly elegant!"

He decided the trapezoid would make the perfect roof for his new home. With great effort, he pushed and dragged the driftwood across the sand until he had built himself a cozy little shelter beside the rocks.

From that day on, Biscuit the crab became famous among the tide pools—not just for his biscuit-colored shell, but for being the only crab who lived beneath a trapezoid roof.

And every evening, as the sun dipped low, Biscuit would sit under his geometric home, content in the knowledge that even the smallest crab could appreciate the beauty of a perfect shape.

**The End.**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about a horse named Never at a Virginia stable, playing on the words "gelding" and "gilding," with a surreal, associative style.
counterfactuals.output:
# Never

At the Virginia stable there is a horse named Never, and Never is a gelding, which is to say Never was made into less so that he might become more manageable, more gentle, more suited to the small hands of children who do not yet know what was taken. But listen: in the low amber hour, when the sun leans hard against the paddock, Never becomes a gilding, his flanks laid over in leaf-thin light, his whole body a manuscript illuminated, a saint's initial burning in the margin of the field.

Never was named for a thing that would not happen. Never bolt. Never buck. Never again the wild inheritance, the stallion's argument with the horizon. And yet the light insists on the opposite spelling, insists on gold, insists Never is always, is forever, is the horse that outlasts the word that unmade him.

The blacksmith comes with fire and the farrier comes with fire and the evening comes with fire, and all of it is a kind of working of metal, a kind of gilding, a hammering of the ordinary into the precious. Never stands for it. Never has learned to stand. His shadow lengthens into another horse entirely, a dark twin galloping east while the body holds its place, gelded, gilded, gone gold at the withers, glossed at the mane, a lamp lit inside an animal that was taught to want nothing.

And the children come with sugar, and the children come with names, and none of them can read the word written all along his back in leaf and light: that what is taken and what is given may arrive by the very same road, may wear the same syllables, may stand in the same field at dusk answering to the same soft impossible name—

Never, Never, come here, boy—

as though calling a thing that cannot be, which is exactly how the gold gets in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece of flash fiction narrated by someone who rode horses in their youth, using strange horse names and a dreamlike, fragmented voice.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Names We Broke

I rode **Cathedral** first, before I knew what falling meant. She had a white blaze shaped like a country that hasn't been discovered yet. My grandmother said: *don't name the wild ones,* but Cathedral came pre-named, arriving like weather.

Some mornings the fog. Some mornings the fog was so thick I rode only by the sound of hooves finding earth.

There was **Tuesday's Widow**, black as the inside of a violin. She threw me twice and I loved her for it. You love the thing that shows you the ground, my father never said, because my father was already a photograph by then, curling at the edges in the tack room where the leather kept its animal smell of having once run.

*Sit deep. Heels down. Chin up—*

I don't remember faces. I remember withers, the warm cathedral of ribs, the way **Barometer** would shudder before rain and I'd know to bring the wash inside.

Once, a horse called **Please**. Just Please. A gray mare going silver going white going toward the color horses turn when they're becoming clouds. I was eleven or I was forty. The barn was burning or the barn was only sunset coming through the slats, laying its ladder-light across the straw.

*You never forget,* they lie. You forget everything except the rhythm. Trot is two beats. Canter is three. Grief is one long held note that doesn't resolve.

**Millstone.** **Aftermath.** **The Understudy**, who only ever wanted to be **Cathedral** and never was.

My legs remember before I do. Some nights they twitch under the sheet, posting to a trot that ended thirty years ago, carrying me toward a fence I clear, always clear, in the dream, the horse beneath me nameless now, or named something I can almost—

Chestnut. Bay. The word *gone* is also a color.

I rode. That much stays. Girl-shaped, stirrup-shaped, thrown and thrown and getting back on because the ground was never the point.

The point was the **going**.

The point was **Please**, turning her cloud-head toward the gate, asking with her whole body: *again?*

And me, always, breathless, small: *yes.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness meditation on memory, fear, and faith, centered on a chestnut gelding and a small mountain.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Chestnut and the Mountain

There was a horse the color of October, of woodsmoke and rusted hinges, and I called him mine though nothing is ever mine, not really, not the light that falls sideways through the aspens nor the breath that leaves us all in white plumes when the cold comes down—

He was afraid of the mountain.

Small thing, that mountain. A hill, a swelling of the earth, a knuckle of granite the old ones would have laughed at. But he saw something there I couldn't see, ears pricked forward, the whole muscled length of him gone electric, gone to trembling, and I remember—

*memory is a horse that startles*

—I remember my grandmother's hands, how they shook near the end, how she said the body remembers what the mind lets go, that fear lives lower down than thought, in the belly, in the blood, in the four hooves planted and refusing.

What did he know that I did not?

The mountain never moved. That was the thing. It only stood there being what it was, indifferent, patient, older than fear itself, older than the first animal that ever flinched from a shadow. And I put my hand flat on his neck and felt the drumming underneath, that ancient telegraph, that message passed down from every horse that ever ran from every hungry thing—

*run, run, the mountain is a lion, the mountain is the dark*

But faith is this: to stand beside the trembling and not need it to be reasonable. To say *I am here* with your palm. To walk toward the small mountain one step and then another, letting the horse decide, letting him carry his terror like a saddlebag until he learns it can be set down—

And he did, one autumn morning, walk that ridge.

Nothing happened. That is the miracle and the whole of it. Nothing happened. The mountain stayed a mountain. The chestnut stayed a chestnut, sweat-dark and blowing, and we came down the other side into a light I have no words for, the kind that makes you understand why the old psalms lifted up their eyes—

*I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills*

—and I think now that all of us are that horse, and all our lives are that small mountain, and the thing we fear has been standing quietly, being nothing, being only itself, waiting for us to walk it and discover we survive.

Memory is a horse.
Fear is a mountain that is smaller than it looks.
And faith—

faith is the hand upon the neck,
the going-forward,
the coming down the far side into morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem where each horse in a stable has an odd name (like Biscuit, Crab, Trapezoid, Never), blending literal stable imagery with abstract reflections on time and sorrow.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Stable of Impossible Horses

In the first stall stands **Biscuit**, who is not warm, who was never warm, whose flanks are the color of a Tuesday you have forgotten. She eats the hours from my open palm and leaves the minutes scattered like oats across the straw.

Beside her, **Crab** paces sideways through his own reflection. He has learned that grief moves laterally, that it does not gallop toward you but arrives at the edge of your vision, wearing the harness of something you almost said. His hooves ring out in the key of low water.

*Listen.*

Here is **Trapezoid**, four-legged proof that no shape holds. He dreams in slanted rain. When the farrier came to measure him, the measurements wept and would not stay still, and this is how we learned that sorrow has no even sides, only the long edge and the short edge and the two that lean away.

And in the far stall, past the lantern's argument with dark, stands **Never**.

Never was foaled from the space between two clock-ticks. Never has the eyes of every horse you sold, every horse that carried you across a river and did not carry you back. When I bring the bridle, Never does not startle. Never has already gone. Never is the mane your fingers move through in the moment before waking, that warm and vanished rope, that yes that was a no.

The stable breathes.

Above us, the loft is stuffed with all the summers—hay-gold, mouse-quiet, packed so tight the light comes through in blades. Below us, the manure of ordinary days, sweet and honest and turning slowly into next.

I muck it out. I muck it out.

Because this is the covenant: you feed the impossible horses, you brush the tangles from their abstract coats, you whisper their strange names into the cathedral of their ears—

*Biscuit. Crab. Trapezoid. Never.*

—and in return they do not carry you anywhere.

They only stand.

They only stand and turn their great heads toward the door, waiting for the one who left, the way time itself is a kind of stable: full of animals that will not be ridden, full of doors we keep unlatching, full of the soft, tremendous patience of things that have all the time there is, and nowhere left to run.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic, allusive short text about loneliness and companionship with a horse, incorporating puns, geographic detail, and cryptic aphorisms.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Withers of Distance

I met my solitude at the Bridle Path, where two roads *canter* off toward nothing much. You'd think a man alone would balk at company, but I have learned to *rein* my expectations low.

---

She came to me near Mane Street, in that county where the Cheval Valley folds itself like a letter no one sends. *A horse is a poem the earth writes in muscle.* I did not saddle her with meaning. She did not ask.

---

They say the lonely heart is a *stable* thing—
that's the first lie. It shifts. It *stalls*.
I've spooked at kindness more than any mare
spooks at her shadow lengthening on the wall.

---

*What gallops toward you may be leaving something else.*

We walked the ridgeline above Fetlock Springs, where the fog wears the hills like a *bit* between its teeth. I told her everything, which is to say I told her nothing, which is the only *tack* an honest silence takes.

---

Here is what the pasture taught:
- Companionship is not the absence of distance but the *grooming* of it.
- The loneliest men ride well; they've had the practice.
- *A friend is a country you can enter without a passport, or a horse.*

---

At dusk we stood, the two of us, near Whinny Cross,
where the old church leans like a saddle no one cinched.
I am not *horsing* around when I confess:
I was less alone than I had ever been,
and *that*—the poets never told me—was the loss.

*What you tame will show you where you're wild.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
